Today the US grid operators respond to FERC’s show-cause orders on large load interconnection - here’s fmr White House “power czar” Peter Lake discussing the significance at @AuroraER_Oxford's recent annual summit:

Oliver Kerr, Managing Director, Aurora Energy Research: A big topic right now is speed to power. If you could wave your magic wand, what would you like to do to see the most gigawatts come online by 2030, and what's getting in the way of that?

Peter Lake, fmr Sr Director, White House: On the load side, we did it. We started with the 403 order from Secretary Wright that was sent in October of 2025 to FERC, directing them to open up a regulatory pathway for fast-track interconnect for data centers. And FERC did a tremendous job. All of the commissioners did a great job, especially Chairman Swett, on getting it moving to get the next part of that regulatory process in the 206 show cause orders.

Which basically says if a data center is willing to curtail their consumption of power during times of grid crisis – that hot summer afternoon, that cold winter morning – if they're willing to do that at the dispatch of the control room, then we'll interconnect you in 60 or 90 days, which is going to be absolutely game-changing for delivering compute…

A 60-day interconnect study, or 90-day, or 100—anything in that range—that's weeks and months, not years and decades. It is going to be fundamentally game-changing for the data center industry, the AI industry, and the power industry for those that get it right. And that is going to be the largest demand response program in history.

SPP was first out of the gates; they're doing a great job on implementing that. MISO is doing a great job on that. I know ERCOT's working on it even though they're outside federal jurisdiction—always got Texas outside federal jurisdiction. So that's on the load side. 

That's the single biggest thing you could do.

note_tweet.text:
$NBIS, $CRWV, AND $IREN ARE GETTING HIT — BUT HAS THE MARKET GONE TOO FAR?

Three major fears are driving the selloff. But the latest earnings reports tell a more complicated story.

1. Neoclouds are running out of financing.

The Q3 numbers challenge that narrative.

• Nebius says customer prepayments and asset-backed financing could cover 75%–85% of its 2027 CapEx.
• CoreWeave expects roughly $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months.
• IREN has secured billions in GPU financing, with customer prepayments covering a significant portion of deployment costs.
Capital isn't free, and these companies still have enormous spending plans. But saying the financing window is completely closed doesn't match what they're reporting.
2. Data center construction is about to hit a political wall.

The midterm results have raised legitimate concerns about electricity costs, grid capacity, and local opposition.

But tighter oversight doesn't automatically mean a nationwide construction ban.

The real question is whether operators can secure power, permits, and community support without pushing costs onto households. That's a challenge — not necessarily the end of AI infrastructure expansion.

3. Jensen Huang's departure means NVIDIA will abandon neoclouds.

This is probably the biggest uncertainty right now.

Huang's resignation is real, and the leadership transition adds another layer of risk. But NVIDIA's strategic interest in expanding demand for its GPUs hasn't automatically disappeared with its former CEO.

Neoclouds remain important customers and infrastructure partners. Still, investors shouldn't assume NVIDIA will keep supporting every financing arrangement or every operator.

Here's what the market may be overlooking:

AI compute demand is still substantial. Customer prepayments are real. Asset-backed financing is still available. And the companies are continuing to expand.

But so are the risks: massive CapEx, interest expense, dilution, execution delays, and regulatory uncertainty.

The selloff may be creating an opportunity — but these stocks aren't risk-free bargains just because they've fallen.

Is this a generational buying opportunity, or is the market finally pricing in risks investors ignored during the AI boom?

note_tweet.text:
THINK ABOUT IT.

- Bill Gates had lots of illicit girlfriends—no problem.

- Elon Musk has multiple children with multiple women—no problem.

- Dario Amodei dated a Chinese woman, Jade Wang, before marrying Cami Clark, who pitched a pornography business to none other than Jeffrey Epstein—no problem.

- But Jensen Huang commits old-fashioned infidelity—and this is such a big problem that he has to resign?

Doesn’t make sense.

Here’s the real story.

CHAPTER ONE: BIDEN’S CHIP WAR
Jensen Huang of Nvidia was puzzled. It was 2022, and his video-graphics processors had become globally popular as the heart of high-end computing across the planet.

But that autumn, Biden violated the World Trade Organization’s most fundamental principles. He ordered the world’s makers of advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment (in the Netherlands, Taiwan and Japan) to stop sales to China.

Biden’s administration implied that the chips were for China’s military gear, but this was a lie. The US’s own security establishment admitted that 99.9 per cent were used for civilian purposes, like medical technology and AI computing.

Huang was dismayed. He could no longer sell Nvidia’s A100 and H100 to China.

CHAPTER TWO: SOLVING A PROBLEM
Jensen Huang was a problem-solver. In February of 2024, Nvidia launched the H20, a made-for-China AI chip less powerful than its US-only top model.

That way he could keep the US government happy but also have something to sell to the Chinese.

Not everyone in the US was happy about this, and export rules fluctuated.

CHAPTER THREE: THE DEEPSEEK MOMENT
In January 2025, a nerdy young man from the Chinese finance industry announced that his firm Deepseek had quickly and cheaply created a high-efficiency open-weight AI.

The implication was huge: the Chinese were finding ways to develop top level AI functionality without massive clusters of top-tier Nvidia GPUs.

Jensen Huang knew he had to respond urgently to keep his place in the China market. He flew to meet trade officials in Beijing in the middle of April and vowed to make "every effort" to serve the Chinese.

The US anti-China hawks had been quietly mobilizing—and made an announcement. In April of 2025, the US banned all export of Jensen Huang’s H20s to China.

Unbelievable! The Nvidia CEO was furious. "Anybody who thought that one chess move to ban China from H20s would cut off their AI ability is deeply uninformed," Huang told an interviewer at a trade meeting in Taipei.

CHAPTER FOUR: HUANG’S SPECIAL SKILL
Then came some rare good news. The Nvidia CEO started lobbying Trump behind the scenes. Huang was a master negotiator – and his efforts proved successful.

In the middle of July, 2025, Huang was back in China—his third trip in 12 months.

Huang appeared without his signature black leather jacket. Instead, he wore a traditional Chinese tang suit, and made some of his speech in Mandarin.

Washington had cleared the way for Nvidia to export the H20 to China, he said. We’re back!

Trump had demanded a cash cut of H20 sales in return for approving the exports—US government policy appeared to be literally for sale.

note_tweet.text:
An AI could follow every safety rule and still make us less capable as humans.

And researchers from Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Oxford are asking us to rethink what AI alignment should mean.

Their paper introduces a fascinating concept: Positive Alignment.

Until now, much of AI alignment has focused on preventing harm.

But what if that's only half the problem?

What if AI shouldn't just avoid harming humanity, but actively help humanity flourish?

Think about it.

An AI that always agrees with you might make you feel supported, while weakening your critical thinking.

An AI that solves every problem for you might increase your productivity, while making you less capable of solving problems independently.

An AI can satisfy your immediate desires without necessarily serving your long-term interests.

And that's where this research becomes truly fascinating.

Perhaps we shouldn't measure AI alignment only by how safe or helpful an answer is.

We should also ask what years of interacting with that AI will do to us.

Will we become wiser, more independent, and more capable?

Or will we gradually outsource our judgment to machines?

But this raises an even deeper philosophical question:

Who gets to decide what "human flourishing" actually means?

The companies developing AI? Governments? Or each individual?

We aren't just designing intelligent machines anymore.

We're making decisions about the kind of humans those machines will help us become.

Paper: https://t.co/ffmAl6L6eT

Mitchell Hashimoto’s Rex post raises a useful point: remote development and production are connected problems, not just two places to run a terminal.

For an AI coding handoff, I’d want four things beside the patch:
• the exact commit and dependency lockfile
• setup steps without embedded secrets
• the test command and its result
• what survives when the remote session disappears

“Works on my agent” should not become the new “works on my machine.”

note_tweet.text:
A thousand years ago, I made a dent in dev envs with “Vagrant.” The most popular request always was “I want Vagrant for remote envs.” I’ve been asked this to this day!! I tried and failed many times. I made things that worked but didn’t work right. Well, Rex is done right. Rex is my answer, finally. 

It’s always lived in the back of my mind no matter what I did. I would come up with something and try it and it didn’t feel right. 

I got really close around 5 years ago to the point I setup a website branding etc (via HashiCorp). But at the last minute I pulled it. It still wasn’t right. I couldn’t explain why and didn’t have a better solution. I just knew it had to be binned. 

Well, Rex is it. This is the real deal. 

Rex is doing for remote development (and a lot more than just dev) what I think a proper solution should’ve done. It’s far more than just a dev tool but I think part of what I knew is once you reach into remote environments that line isn’t clear anymore. You have to solve both remote dev and remote prod. 

Here we go, back to the beginning.
